CABG is a feasible procedure in octogenarians, with acceptable operative risk.
octogenarian patients with coronary artery disease can safely undergo coronary artery bypass surgery with acceptable early and long-term results.
octogenarians are at higher risk than younger patients, but they can benefit from CABG if they have appropriate comorbidities and if they are carefully selected for surgery.

the evaluation of early and late results after CABG in a large series.
the evaluation of the early and late outcomes following CABG in a large series.
the analysis of the results of CABG in a large series, with a mean follow-up of 4 ± 3 years.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
octogenarians with coronary artery disease should not be denied CABG, provided they meet all the criteria of a good candidate for surgery.
CABG in octogenarians is feasible, with acceptable early and late mortality, and with a significant improvement of anginal symptoms and functional status.

CABG in octogenarian patients is safe and feasible, and the early and long-term outcomes are acceptable, provided that a careful patient selection is performed and that a multidisciplinary approach is adopted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of coronary surgery in octogenarian patients are not worse than those in younger patients.
octogenarians are not too old to benefit from CABG if they are carefully selected and treated.
the early and late results after CABG in octogenarians are acceptable, and they should be considered as candidates for CABG.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of CABG in octogenarians is not as high as it is often thought to be.
the results of CABG surgery are good in selected octogenarians and the benefits of surgery are superior to those of percutaneous coronary intervention.
